1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
4	But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
5	
6	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
7	Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
8	Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we investigate \textit{why} this correlation does not reliably translate to selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
9	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.
10	
11	A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
12	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC above 0.81; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
13	For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.

We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
15	Two factors shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples produce identical F1, (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) limits the available headroom; (b)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
16	Our diagnosis is complementary to MBR utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
17	Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
18	Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

25	\end{figure*}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we investigate \textit{why} this correlation does not reliably translate to selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC above 0.81; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Two factors shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples produce identical F1, (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) limits the available headroom; (b)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to MBR utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably predict instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC above 0.81). \textbf{Right}: quality estimation does not translate to selection; all methods approximately match greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation.
    The per-sample vs.\ instance-level distinction determines which signals can, in principle, improve selection.

    \item \textbf{Two empirical mechanisms underlying the correlation-selection gap.}
    Instance degeneracy eliminates headroom; weak LP-quality alignment prevents exploiting the remainder.
    Temperature ablation disentangles the two factors (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); across 23 configurations, degeneracy does not predict LP selection direction ($\rho{=}0.052$), while LP-quality alignment is the primary discriminator. LoRA-rank, supervised signal combinations, and a DeBERTa verifier corroborate the pattern.
    Hidden state probes confirm the gap extends to model-internal representations: higher correlation yields worse selection (\S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}).

    \item \textbf{Practical conditions for LP selection.}
    LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) and scales with $N$; LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$) is the primary predictor of selection viability across our configurations.
    Temperature and training convergence modulate degeneracy, which constrains headroom but does not independently predict selection direction.

    \item \textbf{Prescriptive diagnostic framework.}
    We formalize the two conditions into a practitioner checklist and validate with degeneracy-gated selection (DGS): the framework correctly predicts selection direction across datasets and models, including a cross-model sign reversal on CoNLL explained by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, each serving a distinct role.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed where models achieve ${\approx}$65\% F1.
10	\textbf{Few-NERD} \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (INTRA coarse; 37{,}648 instances, 8 entity types, ${\approx}$75\% F1) provides a low-degeneracy contrast where LP selection succeeds (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
11	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (3{,}453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ${\approx}$91\% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control where limited oracle headroom constrains selection gains.
12	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 52\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary where model capability is insufficient.
13	
14	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
15	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} under identical training procedures, except Few-NERD models which use 3 epochs (early stopping at the best validation checkpoint; a 5-epoch control confirms LP selection remains positive though gains are halved; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
16	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint has a minor train--test mismatch (empty thinking tokens); a quantitative analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
17	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments (ranking stability $\sigma{\leq}0.026$, Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}; sublinear gains beyond $N{=}8$, Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
18	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} (seed protocol: Appendix~\ref{app:multiseed}).

Minor greedy F1 variations across tables reflect protocol differences (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}). Few-NERD uses 3-epoch checkpoints; SciERC and CoNLL use 5 epochs (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).}
102	\label{tab:fewnerd}
103	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
104	\begin{tabular}{@{}lrccccr@{}}
105	\toprule
106	Dataset & $n$ & Greedy & Degen.\% & LP $\rho$ & LP $\Delta$ & $p$ \\
107	\midrule
108	CoNLL & 2{,}756 & .908 & 48.4\% & .302 & $-$0.85\,pp & 1.0 \\
109	SciERC & 529 & .644 & 17.8\% & .205 & $+$0.61\,pp & .193 \\
110	Few-NERD & 32{,}565 & .748 & 13.8\% & .421 & $\mathbf{+1.39}$\,pp & ${<}.001$ \\
111	\bottomrule
112	\end{tabular}}
113	\end{table}
114	
115	Few-NERD (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}) confirms that LP selection effectiveness is inversely associated with degeneracy.
116	Under standard early stopping (3 epochs for Few-NERD vs.\ 5 for SciERC/CoNLL), Few-NERD degeneracy is 13.8\%, and LP achieves $+1.39$~pp ($p{<}0.001$, 3-seed mean ${\pm}0.04$~pp), while all structural signals degrade selection (VC $-1.79$, SJ $-2.14$~pp).
117	Training convergence modulates degeneracy: a 5-epoch Few-NERD control raises degeneracy to 31\% and halves LP gains, though selection remains positive (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
118	
119	\paragraph{Empirical pattern for LP selection.}
120	The cross-dataset gradient is consistent with an inverse relationship (48.4\% $\to$ $-0.85$~pp, 17.8\% $\to$ $+0.61$~pp, 13.8\% $\to$ $+1.39$~pp; $n{=}3$ datasets, exploratory given 5+ confounds; Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}), with supporting evidence from per-entity-type analysis within Few-NERD ($n{=}8$, $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$; entity types share model, tokenizer, and temperature, so effective degrees of freedom may be lower than 6).
121	Low degeneracy alone does not ensure selection gains: the LoRA-rank ablation (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) reduces degeneracy to 7.2\% yet LP does not improve selection because $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){\approx}0.24$.
122	Few-NERD exhibits both favorable factors: low degeneracy (13.8\%) and strong alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$; per-type detail in Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
123	All five signals achieve positive QE on Few-NERD (LP $\rho{=}0.42$, VC $0.39$), yet only LP translates QE into selection; the gap confirms that strong instance-level QE cannot rank candidates within an instance.
124	Conditional analysis on the favorable subset (non-degenerate instances whose within-instance LP range exceeds the dataset-specific median) yields $+2.47$~pp on SciERC (CI $[+0.30, +4.70]$) and a marginal positive trend on Few-NERD ($+0.63$~pp, CI $[-0.02, +1.30]$); CoNLL remains negative ($-1.78$~pp), consistent with ceiling-regime degeneracy even within the favorable subset (Appendix~\ref{app:conditional_decomp}).
125	
126	\begin{figure}[t]
127	\centering
128	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_degeneracy_lp_scatter.pdf}
129	\caption{Instance degeneracy vs.\ LP selection gain. Blue circles: cross-dataset ($n{=}3$, exploratory). Orange triangles: per-entity-type within Few-NERD ($n{=}8$, $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$; types share model and tokenizer). The dashed line at ${\sim}$15\%\protect\footnotemark{} separates regimes where LP improves (left) vs.\ shows insufficient evidence (right).}
130	\label{fig:degeneracy_scatter}
131	\end{figure}
132	
133	\footnotetext{Boundary between Person (13.4\%, $+1.25$~pp) and Art (19.8\%, $-0.17$~pp).}
134	
135	\paragraph{LP selection scales with sample budget.}
136	Doubling $N$ from 8 to 16 on Few-NERD yields $+0.52$~pp (paired $p{=}0.003$, CI $[+0.17, +0.87]$), driven by reduced degeneracy (14.6\% $\to$ 7.0\%) expanding headroom (12.1 $\to$ 15.4~pp), while LP ranking quality remains stable ($\rho{\approx}0.62$).
137	Structural signals remain uniformly negative at $N{=}16$; the gap persists regardless of sample budget.
138	
139	%% ============================================================
140	\subsection{Robustness}
141	\label{sec:robustness_main}
142	
143	Consistency signals are robust across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ with sublinear $N$-scaling gains (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}); LP shows the largest temperature sensitivity ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.044$).
144	Signal rankings are stable across seeds (Kendall's $W{=}1.0$ at $N{=}8$; $m{=}3$ raters, interpret with caution given low $m$; exact $p{\approx}0.028$; Table~\ref{tab:ranking-stability}).
145	NER calibration is reasonable (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).
146	
147	\begin{table}[t]
148	\centering
149	\small
150	\caption{Scale ablation: Qwen3-8B vs.\ 4B NER quality estimation ($\rho$; $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seed${=}42$). 8B values identical to Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}; 4B uses matched evaluation protocol. RE scale ablation in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.}
151	\label{tab:scale_ablation}
152	\begin{tabular}{@{}ll cc r@{}}
153	\toprule
154	& & \textbf{8B} & \textbf{4B} & $\Delta$ \\
155	\midrule
156	CoNLL & SJ & .436 & .422 & $-$.014 \\
157	      & FK & .400 & .418 & $+$.018 \\
158	SciERC & SJ & .360 & .422 & $+$.062 \\
159	       & FK & .267 & .326 & $+$.059 \\
160	\bottomrule
161	\end{tabular}
162	\end{table}
163	
164	\paragraph{Scale robustness.}
165	With Qwen3-4B (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), QE is comparable (mean $|\Delta\rho|{=}0.042$), yet selection remains below greedy despite 13.0~pp headroom. Task difficulty is a stronger predictor than model scale within the 3B--8B range (Appendix~\ref{app:llama3b}).
166	Degeneracy scales with capability: 8B shows 17.8\% vs.\ 4B's 10.4\% on SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
167	
168	\paragraph{LoRA-rank ablation.}
169	Training with LoRA rank${=}8$ (vs.\ 32) lowers degeneracy from 17.8\% to 7.2\% and increases headroom to 16.0~pp, but LP does not improve selection (0.635 vs.\ greedy 0.640).
170	This ablation conflates diversity with model capacity (rank 8 has fewer trainable parameters); within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){\approx}0.24$ remains too weak despite wider LP spread (0.057 vs.\ 0.041 nats).
171	Temperature manipulation (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) provides a cleaner test by altering diversity without changing capacity, and yields the same conclusion: both low degeneracy and adequate alignment appear independently associated with selection success.
172	
173	\paragraph{Supervised signal combination.}
174	Supervised classifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) trained on all five signals (5-fold CV, 3-seed mean, SciERC, $N{=}16$, $+17.9$~pp headroom) all perform at or below greedy (F1${=}0.644$; LR: $-0.4$~pp; MLP: $-1.6$~pp; RF: $-3.1$~pp).
175	Adding pairwise interaction features does not help (AUROC 0.634 vs.\ 0.638).
176	To test whether richer representations could close the gap, we train a DeBERTa-v3-base verifier that encodes input-output pairs and predicts per-sample F1.
177	DeBERTa achieves $\rho{=}0.329{\pm}0.087$ (5-fold CV, 3 seeds). Despite moderate quality prediction, selection utility is poor: on SciERC, DeBERTa closes $-26.5{\pm}26.5$\% of the oracle gap (13 of 15 runs negative; vs.\ LP's $+4.2{\pm}10.7$\%); on Few-NERD, DeBERTa recovers only $+3.5$\% (single 80/20 split; vs.\ LP's $+16.3$\%).
178	Cross-dataset transfer fails entirely ($-27$\% to $-72$\% gap closure).
179	Neither handcrafted signal combinations (LR, MLP, RF on 5 scalar signals) nor learned text representations close the selection gap; only model-internal log-probability provides meaningful selection signal, consistent with an information asymmetry between the generating model and external observers.
180	
181	%% ============================================================
182	\subsection{Probing the Information Gap}
183	\label{sec:hidden_probe}
184	
185	The preceding negative results suggest the bottleneck is model-internal rather than a feature engineering problem.
186	We test this directly by training probes on the generating model's hidden representations.
187	
188	\paragraph{Setup.}
189	For each of $N{=}8$ samples per instance, we extract the mean-pooled final-layer hidden state ($d{=}4096$) from the generating Qwen3-8B model and train a linear probe and a two-layer MLP (hidden dim${=}256$) to predict per-sample F1 (5-fold CV, 3 seeds).
190	
191	\begin{table}[t]
192	\centering
193	\small
194	\caption{Hidden state probes vs.\ LP for sample selection (5-fold CV ${\times}$ 3 seeds). $\rho$: Spearman correlation with per-sample F1. Sel.\ F1: selection F1. Gap\%: oracle gap closure. SciERC greedy${=}0.644$, oracle${=}0.775$.}
195	\label{tab:hidden_probe}
196	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
197	\begin{tabular}{@{}l ccc cc@{}}
198	\toprule
199	& \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{SciERC}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Few-NERD}} \\
200	\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6}
201	Method & $\rho$ & Sel.\ F1 & Gap\% & $\rho$ & Gap\% \\
202	\midrule
203	LP & .283 & $\mathbf{.650}$ & $+$4.8 & .606 & 12.3 \\
204	Hidden Linear & $.179{\pm}.019$ & $.613{\pm}.002$ & $-$23.4 & \multicolumn{2}{c}{---} \\
205	Hidden MLP & $\mathbf{.388{\pm}.013}$ & $.637{\pm}.003$ & $-$5.1 & $\mathbf{.629{\pm}.007}$ & 11.7 \\
206	\bottomrule
207	\end{tabular}}
208	\end{table}
209	
210	\paragraph{Cross-dataset asymmetry.}
211	On SciERC, the MLP probe achieves higher quality correlation than LP ($\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ $0.283$, $+37$\%); hidden states encode information beyond what LP captures.
212	Yet higher correlation does not yield better selection: MLP selection F1 ($0.637$) falls below LP's ($0.650$), with gap closure turning negative ($-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; Table~\ref{tab:hidden_probe}).
213	The linear probe performs worse still ($\rho{=}0.179$, gap closure $-23.4$\%).
214	On Few-NERD, the MLP provides no increment over LP (gap closure $11.7$\% vs.\ $12.3$\%).
215	A learned token-level LP aggregator (1D CNN over per-token log-probabilities) matches mean LP on Few-NERD (gap closure $56.4$\% vs.\ $55.8$\%), confirming that LP's bottleneck is not token aggregation.
216	The correlation-selection gap thus extends to model-internal representations: in the high-capability regime (greedy F1${=}0.644$), inter-sample F1 differences are small enough that improved ranking provides no marginal selection value, consistent with the capability-diversity tension (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
217	
218	\phantomsection\label{sec:selection_results}
219	%% Framework validation (DGS) is presented in Discussion §5 to save space
220

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Implications.}
4	All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
5	For selection, LP tends to achieve gains when both factors are present (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
6	The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.
7	
8	\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
9	Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
10	Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 48.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
11	LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
12	Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
13	An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
14	Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.
15	
16	\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
17	Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).
18	
19	\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
20	QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).
21	Temperature manipulation provides the primary evidence that both factors appear independently associated with selection success: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
22	Approximate boundaries from our data: degeneracy ${<}$15\% and $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}) \gtrsim 0.3$; temperature and training convergence are controllable levers (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).
23	
24	\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
25	Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 86.5\% vs.\ Qwen 48.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
26	For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
27	This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.
28	
29	\paragraph{From diagnosis to selection.}\label{sec:selection_method}
30	A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS) that gates on within-instance LP range yields modest gains but cannot overcome weak alignment (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}).
31	Entity-level majority voting (${\geq}N/2$ threshold) yields $+0.76$~pp on SciERC but is negative on CoNLL and Few-NERD; uniformly negative on degenerate subsets (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).
32	MBR selection is uniformly negative except under high diversity (SciERC $T{=}1.2$, $+1.8$~pp).
33	These findings yield a prescriptive checklist: apply LP selection only when degeneracy is low and $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ adequate, unlike adaptive SC \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive, kim2026reasc} that gates on answer agreement.
34	Degeneracy-gated selection (DGS) diagnoses when selection is viable: positive on Few-NERD ($+0.92$~pp, both conditions met), non-significant on SciERC ($+0.71$~pp, weak alignment).
35	The strongest validation is the CoNLL cross-model contrast: Qwen DGS is negative ($-0.81$~pp, LP harms even non-degenerate instances, $\rho{\sim}0.2$) while LLaMA DGS is positive ($+0.14$~pp, non-degenerate LP $+1.37$~pp); the same task yields opposite directions due to LP-quality alignment alone.
36

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications.}
All signals achieve positive quality estimation across non-collapsed datasets, with rankings stable across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
For selection, LP tends to achieve gains when both factors are present (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); structural signals uniformly degrade selection.
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Two mechanisms block selection: \textit{instance degeneracy} (consensus-proximity) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (per-sample).
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$), but 17.8\% (SciERC) to 48.4\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all samples, eliminating headroom entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
LP is severely compressed (median range 0.041 nats; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ ranging from 0.262 (SciERC) to 0.667 (Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:within_rho}).
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), within-instance $\rho$ rises to 0.39 and LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}).
An oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it (Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, \ref{app:vc_quartile}).
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists (SciERC MLP $\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ LP $0.283$, $+37$\%), but the correlation-selection gap persists (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; \S\ref{sec:hidden_probe}): the bottleneck is diminishing marginal returns on selection, not information loss.

\paragraph{LP compression mechanisms.}
Four non-mutually-exclusive mechanisms contribute (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); entity-token LP shows $4{\times}$ higher variance yet performs worse; compression operates at the representation level, not token aggregation (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_token_lp}).

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
QE signals collapse at the low-resource boundary (WNUT-17, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}) and LP degrades selection at the ceiling (CoNLL, degeneracy 48--87\%, $-0.85$~pp).
Temperature manipulation provides the primary evidence that both factors appear independently associated with selection success: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve because alignment remains weak ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the SciERC epoch curve corroborates this (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}).
Approximate boundaries from our data: degeneracy ${<}$15\% and $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}) \gtrsim 0.3$; temperature and training convergence are controllable levers (Tables~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), while calibration cannot improve selection (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\paragraph{Capability-diversity tension.}
Degeneracy rises with model scale (4B: 10.4\% vs.\ 8B: 17.8\%; Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), training convergence (Few-NERD: 14\% at 3 epochs to 31\% at 5; Tables~\ref{tab:fewnerd}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}, \ref{tab:epoch_scierc}), and model family (LLaMA 86.5\% vs.\ Qwen 48.4\% on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
For structured IE, the same training progress that reduces error also reduces the output diversity on which selection depends \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
This pattern is observational and does not establish causality, but the consistency across independent axes suggests a systematic relationship: as models improve, the window for test-time selection narrows.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to selection.}\label{sec:selection_method}
A degeneracy-aware LP strategy (DALS) that gates on within-instance LP range yields modest gains but cannot overcome weak alignment (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}).
Entity-level majority voting (${\geq}N/2$ threshold) yields $+0.76$~pp on SciERC but is negative on CoNLL and Few-NERD; uniformly negative on degenerate subsets (Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).
MBR selection is uniformly negative except under high diversity (SciERC $T{=}1.2$, $+1.8$~pp).
These findings yield a prescriptive checklist: apply LP selection only when degeneracy is low and $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ adequate, unlike adaptive SC \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive, kim2026reasc} that gates on answer agreement.
Degeneracy-gated selection (DGS) diagnoses when selection is viable: positive on Few-NERD ($+0.92$~pp, both conditions met), non-significant on SciERC ($+0.71$~pp, weak alignment).
The strongest validation is the CoNLL cross-model contrast: Qwen DGS is negative ($-0.81$~pp, LP harms even non-degenerate instances, $\rho{\sim}0.2$) while LLaMA DGS is positive ($+0.14$~pp, non-degenerate LP $+1.37$~pp); the same task yields opposite directions due to LP-quality alignment alone.

\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$; the two selection rules are equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{SJ normalizer robustness.}
Equation~\ref{eq:sj} uses $\max(|g_i|, |g_j|)$ as the denominator; an alternative is the union size $|g_i \cup g_j|$.
Table~\ref{tab:sj_normalizer} compares the two normalizers across all six model--dataset combinations ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seed${=}42$): $|\Delta\rho|{<}0.01$ in every case, the choice between max and union normalization does not affect conclusions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{SJ normalizer comparison (Spearman $\rho$; $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seed${=}42$). Max: $\max(|g_i|,|g_j|)$; Union: $|g_i \cup g_j|$.}
\label{tab:sj_normalizer}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll ccc@{}}
\toprule
Dataset & Model & $\rho$(max) & $\rho$(union) & $\Delta\rho$ \\
\midrule
CoNLL & Qwen3-8B & .436 & .438 & $-$.002 \\
CoNLL & Qwen3-4B & .422 & .421 & $+$.000 \\
CoNLL & LLaMA-8B & .431 & .432 & $-$.000 \\
SciERC & Qwen3-8B & .360 & .365 & $-$.005 \\
SciERC & Qwen3-4B & .422 & .423 & $-$.001 \\
SciERC & LLaMA-8B & .363 & .372 & $-$.009 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, consistent with the NER structural advantage; on full-set RE, however, the SJ--FK difference is non-significant ($\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.005$, $p{=}0.53$; preliminary).
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations: SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$). This holds despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Five confidence signals achieve reliable NER quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC above 0.81), but selection gains are associated with low degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment (approximate thresholds: ${<}$15\% and $\rho \gtrsim 0.3$); LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD where both hold.
Hidden state probes confirm richer information exists but the gap persists; content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} may be needed to close it.
As models improve, degeneracy rises and the selection window narrows.

201	On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
202	On the conditional set, where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs, exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
203	The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

228	\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
229	Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to four additional configurations.
230	On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of single-sample (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
231	On CoNLL, 48--87\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples; this reflects a ceiling effect (single-sample F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure, and selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

250	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
251	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
252	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
253	Structural signals use $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, each additional comparison yields diminishing information.
254	This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
255	For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound (more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate), but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
256	The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.
257	
258	\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
259	While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
260	VC achieves the largest gain over single-sample ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
261	These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
262	This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions (high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence), signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

308	\section{Diversity and Selection Analysis}\label{app:diversity}

317	\paragraph{Output diversity quantification.}
318	Table~\ref{tab:diversity} summarizes output diversity across configurations.
319	On SciERC, output diversity is substantial: Qwen produces 43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct out of $N{=}8$), with per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.144 and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.

321	On CoNLL, diversity collapses: 59\% (Qwen) to 89\% (LLaMA) of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples; this reflects a ceiling effect where single-sample F1 already exceeds 0.90.

326	\small
327	\caption{Output diversity across configurations ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). ``Identical'' = fraction of instances with all $N$ outputs identical. ``Unique'' = mean fraction of distinct outputs per instance.}

342	\paragraph{Oracle-improvable fraction.}
343	Across SciERC configurations, 39--42\% of instances contain at least one sample with F1 exceeding single-sample\footnote{Oracle-improvable and diversity-stratified analyses use $n{=}529$ (excluding instances with empty gold annotations; see \S\ref{sec:evaluation}); the diversity quantification in Table~\ref{tab:diversity} uses the full test set.}: Qwen NER 42.0\% (222/529, mean headroom $+$31.9~pp among improvable instances), Qwen RE 41.3\% (164/397, $+$45.3~pp), LLaMA NER 39.3\% (208/529, $+$33.7~pp).
344	On CoNLL, only 4--9\% of instances are improvable, consistent with the ceiling effect.
345	
346	\paragraph{Diversity-stratified selection gap.}
347	On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below single-sample, and LP, the only per-sample signal, achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
348	LLaMA replicates this pattern: on its high-diversity subset ($n{=}186$), oracle headroom reaches $+$20.1~pp while consistency signals remain at or below single-sample and LP captures only $+$2.0~pp.
349	This rules out insufficient diversity as an explanation for the correlation-selection gap.

371	\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
372	The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
373	Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
374	The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
375	These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom, introducing circularity: $\delta$ is anchored to the very quantity it contextualizes.
376	We address this below with externally anchored equivalence margins.
377	The breakpoint $\delta^*$, the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST, ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
378	On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to single-sample (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
379	On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
380	The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

383	\centering
384	\small
385	\caption{TOST equivalence testing: signals vs.\ single-sample on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). \checkmark: equivalent at $p{<}0.05$; \texttimes: not equivalent. $\Delta$: mean F1 difference (signal $-$ single-sample).}

402	\paragraph{External equivalence margins.}
403	The oracle-headroom anchors above introduce circularity, as a reviewer correctly noted: $\delta$ is calibrated against the very quantity it contextualizes.
404	To resolve this, we supplement with three externally grounded margins:
405	(1) $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}$: the bootstrapped standard error of single-sample F1 (0.43--1.33~pp depending on configuration), which represents measurement noise;
406	(2) $\delta_{\mathrm{practical}}{=}0.5$~pp, the threshold below which NER differences are considered negligible \cite{ratinov2009design};
407	(3) $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}{=}1.0$~pp, the approximate significant-difference threshold established in NER evaluation methodology \cite{bergkirkpatrick2012empirical}.
408	
409	Results under these external anchors diverge sharply by configuration.
410	On LLaMA CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), all signals pass equivalence at every $\delta$ ($p{<}0.001$), consistent with the near-zero selection deltas ($|\Delta|{\leq}0.1$~pp) and tight CIs at this sample size.
411	On Qwen CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), no signal passes at any external $\delta$: selection F1 degrades by 0.9--1.5~pp relative to single-sample, which exceeds even $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}$.
412	On SciERC NER ($n{=}529$), only SJ passes at $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}{=}1.33$~pp (the widest SEM bound); all other signals and tighter margins fail.
413	These external anchors confirm that the equivalence conclusion is configuration-dependent: LLaMA CoNLL selection is robustly equivalent to single-sample under any reasonable margin, while SciERC and Qwen CoNLL selection shows detectable degradation at externally calibrated thresholds.
414	
415	\paragraph{Multiple comparison considerations.}\label{app:multiple_comparisons}
416	Our primary selection analysis involves ${\sim}$20 comparisons (5 signals $\times$ 3--4 configurations).
417	Since all primary selection results are non-significant ($p{>}0.05$), applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction can only make these results more conservative, strengthening the ``no signal beats greedy'' conclusion.
418	The sole positive finding, the non-tied LP subset ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), survives Bonferroni correction over 5 signal comparisons ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.020 < 0.05$), as noted in the main text footnote.
419	For quality estimation signal rankings, differences between the top signals (e.g., VC vs.\ SJ on SciERC) should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as statistically confirmed orderings, given the limited power of 3-seed comparisons.
420	
421	\section{Multi-Seed Stability}\label{app:multiseed}
422	
423	Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} reports quality estimation metrics across three random seeds for both model families on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
424	On NER, the signal ranking VC${>}$SJ${>}$EM${>}$FK${>}$LP is identical across all six model-seed combinations, with $\sigma{\leq}0.025$ for all signals (rankings are stable across our 3 seeds, though statistical power with $n{=}3$ is limited).
425	On RE (Qwen only, preliminary), VC remains the top signal ($\rho{=}0.309{\pm}0.024$), but LP rises to \#2 ($\rho{=}0.297{\pm}0.022$), above FK, SJ, and EM. This reversal from the NER ranking reflects RE's higher sensitivity to per-sample scoring.
426	LLaMA absolute values are systematically lower than Qwen on NER, consistent with the directionally-consistent-but-magnitude-dependent characterization in the main text.
427	
428	\begin{table}[t]
429	\centering
430	\small
431	\caption{Multi-seed quality estimation on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seeds: 42, 123, 456). NER: both models; RE: Qwen only (preliminary). Signal ranking is stable across seeds ($\sigma{\leq}0.025$). $\sigma$ is population standard deviation over 3 seeds.}
432	\label{tab:multiseed}
433	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
434	\toprule

EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations: SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$). This holds despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set, where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs, exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

VC's high full-set $\rho{=}0.724$ is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, $p{=}0.49$), while LP's conditional $\rho{=}0.350$ is the highest among all signals on the non-zero subset, full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to four additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of single-sample (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On CoNLL, 48--87\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples; this reflects a ceiling effect (single-sample F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure, and selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals use $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, each additional comparison yields diminishing information.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound (more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate), but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
VC achieves the largest gain over single-sample ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions (high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence), signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

The SJ--LP gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$) is clearly significant, the structural advantage reported in \S\ref{sec:qe_results} is robust.
The VC--SJ gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.019$) is not significant; these two structural signals perform comparably.
The SJ--EM gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.065$) is borderline significant, with the CI lower bound at $+0.003$ and upper bound at $+0.130$.

\section{Diversity and Selection Analysis}\label{app:diversity}

\begin{figure*}[t]

RE selection results in Table~\ref{tab:selection}.}

\paragraph{Output diversity quantification.}
Table~\ref{tab:diversity} summarizes output diversity across configurations.
On SciERC, output diversity is substantial: Qwen produces 43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct out of $N{=}8$), with per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.144 and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.
LLaMA shows similar diversity (39\% unique, F1 std 0.11).
On CoNLL, diversity collapses: 59\% (Qwen) to 89\% (LLaMA) of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples; this reflects a ceiling effect where single-sample F1 already exceeds 0.90.
WNUT-17 shows 55\% identical outputs, driven by the 52\% zero-F1 rate.

\paragraph{Oracle-improvable fraction.}
Across SciERC configurations, 39--42\% of instances contain at least one sample with F1 exceeding single-sample\footnote{Oracle-improvable and diversity-stratified analyses use $n{=}529$ (excluding instances with empty gold annotations; see \S\ref{sec:evaluation}); the diversity quantification in Table~\ref{tab:diversity} uses the full test set.}: Qwen NER 42.0\% (222/529, mean headroom $+$31.9~pp among improvable instances), Qwen RE 41.3\% (164/397, $+$45.3~pp), LLaMA NER 39.3\% (208/529, $+$33.7~pp).
On CoNLL, only 4--9\% of instances are improvable, consistent with the ceiling effect.

\paragraph{Diversity-stratified selection gap.}
On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below single-sample, and LP, the only per-sample signal, achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
LLaMA replicates this pattern: on its high-diversity subset ($n{=}186$), oracle headroom reaches $+$20.1~pp while consistency signals remain at or below single-sample and LP captures only $+$2.0~pp.
This rules out insufficient diversity as an explanation for the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom, introducing circularity: $\delta$ is anchored to the very quantity it contextualizes.
We address this below with externally anchored equivalence margins.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$, the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST, ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to single-sample (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\label{tab:tost}

\paragraph{External equivalence margins.}
The oracle-headroom anchors above introduce circularity, as a reviewer correctly noted: $\delta$ is calibrated against the very quantity it contextualizes.
To resolve this, we supplement with three externally grounded margins:
(1) $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}$: the bootstrapped standard error of single-sample F1 (0.43--1.33~pp depending on configuration), which represents measurement noise;
(2) $\delta_{\mathrm{practical}}{=}0.5$~pp, the threshold below which NER differences are considered negligible \cite{ratinov2009design};
(3) $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}{=}1.0$~pp, the approximate significant-difference threshold established in NER evaluation methodology \cite{bergkirkpatrick2012empirical}.

Results under these external anchors diverge sharply by configuration.
On LLaMA CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), all signals pass equivalence at every $\delta$ ($p{<}0.001$), consistent with the near-zero selection deltas ($|\Delta|{\leq}0.1$~pp) and tight CIs at this sample size.
On Qwen CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), no signal passes at any external $\delta$: selection F1 degrades by 0.9--1.5~pp relative to single-sample, which exceeds even $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}$.
On SciERC NER ($n{=}529$), only SJ passes at $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}{=}1.33$~pp (the widest SEM bound); all other signals and tighter margins fail.
These external anchors confirm that the equivalence conclusion is configuration-dependent: LLaMA CoNLL selection is robustly equivalent to single-sample under any reasonable margin, while SciERC and Qwen CoNLL selection shows detectable degradation at externally calibrated thresholds.

\paragraph{Multiple comparison considerations.}\label{app:multiple_comparisons}
Our primary selection analysis involves ${\sim}$20 comparisons (5 signals $\times$ 3--4 configurations).
Since all primary selection results are non-significant ($p{>}0.05$), applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction can only make these results more conservative, strengthening the ``no signal beats greedy'' conclusion.
The sole positive finding, the non-tied LP subset ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), survives Bonferroni correction over 5 signal comparisons ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.020 < 0.05$), as noted in the main text footnote.
For quality estimation signal rankings, differences between the top signals (e.g., VC vs.\ SJ on SciERC) should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as statistically confirmed orderings, given the limited power of 3-seed comparisons.

\section{Multi-Seed Stability}\label{app:multiseed}

Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} reports quality estimation metrics across three random seeds for both model families on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
On NER, the signal ranking VC${>}$SJ${>}$EM${>}$FK${>}$LP is identical across all six model-seed combinations, with $\sigma{\leq}0.025$ for all signals (rankings are stable across our 3 seeds, though statistical power with $n{=}3$ is limited).
On RE (Qwen only, preliminary), VC remains the top signal ($\rho{=}0.309{\pm}0.024$), but LP rises to \#2 ($\rho{=}0.297{\pm}0.022$), above FK, SJ, and EM. This reversal from the NER ranking reflects RE's higher sensitivity to per-sample scoring.
LLaMA absolute values are systematically lower than Qwen on NER, consistent with the directionally-consistent-but-magnitude-dependent characterization in the main text.

487	\paragraph{Prompt template.}
488	For NER, we use a structured prompt:
489	\begin{quote}
490	\small
491	\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
492	\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
493	Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
494	Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
495	\end{quote}
496	RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.
497	
498	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
499	Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{dong2024xgrammar, willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
500	This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}
501	
502	\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}
503	
504	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
505	We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.
506	
507	\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
508	Empty thinking tokens (mean 4.5 per sample) constitute 2.1\% of tokens on SciERC.
509	The estimated LP shift is 0.001 nats per token (2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range of 0.041 nats).
510	Because all samples share identical thinking-token LP offsets, cumulative LP rankings are invariant; mean LP changes selection for ${<}1.5\%$ of instances.
511	
512	\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
513	All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
514	Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.
515	
516	\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
517	CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
518	If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
519	Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions at both temperatures (86.8\% at $T{=}1.0$, 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$) than SciERC (60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.
520

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:
\begin{quote}
\small
\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
\end{quote}
RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{dong2024xgrammar, willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.

\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
Empty thinking tokens (mean 4.5 per sample) constitute 2.1\% of tokens on SciERC.
The estimated LP shift is 0.001 nats per token (2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range of 0.041 nats).
Because all samples share identical thinking-token LP offsets, cumulative LP rankings are invariant; mean LP changes selection for ${<}1.5\%$ of instances.

\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.

\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions at both temperatures (86.8\% at $T{=}1.0$, 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$) than SciERC (60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.

The NER pattern reveals two complementary failure modes rather than a monotonic relationship between consistency and selection gain:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Q4 ceiling effect.} High-consistency instances (mean VC${=}0.92$) have oracle headroom of only 4.78~pp. Samples have already converged, leaving little room for any signal to improve selection.
\item \textbf{Q1--Q2 noise.} Low-consistency instances retain large headroom (14--17~pp) but LP rankings are unreliable, and LP rankings produce inconsistent $\Delta$ signs across quartiles.
\end{itemize}

On $^\dagger$RE, the pattern differs: Q4 LP achieves $+4.01$~pp; LP may recover selection ability when high consistency coincides with structured output diversity. This is a single-dataset observation and should be interpreted cautiously.

On CoNLL NER, Q3--Q4 instances have VC${=}1.0$ (all samples identical), and $\Delta{=}0$ universally; this ceiling effect is even more extreme than SciERC Q4.

\section{Exploratory Extension to Relation Extraction}\label{app:re_extension}

We extend the NER evaluation to relation extraction (RE) on SciERC as an exploratory single-benchmark analysis.

All RE results use Qwen3-8B unless noted; single-seed ($\text{seed}{=}42$) for $N{=}8$ analyses, 3-seed for $N{=}16$.

774	\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}
775	
776	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
777	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
778	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy, the core of the correlation-selection gap.
779	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
780	
781	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
782	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
783	On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
784	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
785	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
786	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
787	The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472: 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, and the newly non-tied subset shows a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
788	Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible. Score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
789	Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

1113	\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
1114	When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
1115	The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (single-sample F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.
1116	
1117	\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
1118	The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
1119	The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (single-sample NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
1120	Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
1121	These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs, a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}) and not evidence against signal utility.
1122	
1123	\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
1124	The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
1125	This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

\paragraph{$N$-scaling: selection headroom vs.\ selection gain.}
Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection} traces the effect of sample count on degeneracy, oracle headroom, and per-signal selection gain.
Oracle headroom grows roughly linearly with $N$ ($+4.4$~pp at $N{=}2$ to $+20.0$~pp at $N{=}32$).
LP selection improves monotonically with $N$ ($+0.39$~pp at $N{=}8$ to $+0.95$~pp at $N{=}32$), but even at $N{=}32$, where degeneracy falls to 4\% and oracle headroom reaches ${\sim}20$~pp, the best signal captures less than 5\% of the available improvement.

VC selection degrades with increasing $N$ ($-2.66$~pp at $N{=}2$ to $-4.35$~pp at $N{=}32$), consistent with mode-seeking bias in voting-based selection as the candidate pool grows.

LP $\rho$ peaks at $T{=}0.8$ ($0.253$) then degrades to $0.196$ at $T{=}1.2$.
This divergence confirms that LP compression is model-intrinsic: higher temperature increases between-instance LP variance (benefiting structural signals) but does not resolve within-instance compression, degrading LP's discriminative power.
Inter-sample agreement ($\kappa$) decreases monotonically ($0.577$ to $0.356$); higher temperature generates more diverse outputs. Mean sample F1 also decreases ($0.636$ to $0.594$), consistent with the quality--diversity trade-off.
The $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$ comparison in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} is consistent with the trends reported here.

\paragraph{Temperature controls degeneracy and LP spread.}
Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy} reports instance degeneracy (constant F1, gold-filtered) and median within-instance LP range across four temperatures on SciERC.
Both quantities are strictly monotonic in $T$: degeneracy falls from 41.4\% ($T{=}0.5$) to 14.9\% ($T{=}1.2$), while LP range increases from 0.015 to 0.058 nats.
Temperature thus provides a direct lever for practitioners to shift the degeneracy regime.
However, even at $T{=}1.2$ where degeneracy (14.9\%) approaches Few-NERD levels (${\sim}$14\%), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ remains at 0.225, far below Few-NERD's ${\sim}$0.5.
This confirms that temperature controls degeneracy (the first factor) but cannot improve LP-quality alignment (the second factor), which is largely determined by task structure and remains relatively stable across generation configurations (\S\ref{app:epoch_confound}); both factors appear associated with selection success in the regimes we tested and vary independently.

\section{Cross-Dataset OOD Analysis}\label{app:ood}

To test whether confidence signals generalize under domain shift, we evaluate models on out-of-distribution data: a SciERC-trained model applied to CoNLL instances (wider$\to$narrower schema) and vice versa (Table~\ref{tab:ood}).

\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (single-sample F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.

\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (single-sample NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs, a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}) and not evidence against signal utility.

\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

\paragraph{Severe overconfidence.}
VerbConf exhibits extreme score compression: mean confidence is 8.58/10 on SciERC (single-sample F1${=}0.645$) and 9.24/10 on CoNLL (single-sample F1${=}0.904$), with most scores concentrated in the 8--10 range.
This compression is more severe than LP (which spans a 0.041-nat median range); score compression is a general property of model self-assessment, not an artifact of log-probability computation.

\paragraph{QE--selection decoupling.}
VerbConf achieves higher $\rho$ than LP on both datasets (SciERC: 0.297 vs.\ 0.205; CoNLL: 0.337 vs.\ 0.316) and competitive AUROC (SciERC: 0.681 vs.\ 0.578; CoNLL: 0.747 vs.\ 0.753), yet yields the worst selection among all signals ($\Delta{=}{-}2.45$~pp on SciERC, $-1.93$~pp on CoNLL).
This dissociation further demonstrates the correlation-selection gap: a signal can rank instances by expected quality without being able to discriminate candidates within an instance.
The AUROC--$\rho$ decoupling on CoNLL (LP leads AUROC at 0.753 while VerbConf leads $\rho$ at 0.337) reflects differing sensitivity to binary vs.\ ordinal discrimination.

\section{Few-NERD Full Results}\label{app:fewnerd}

Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd_full} reports the complete Few-NERD INTRA coarse evaluation (Qwen3-8B, LoRA rank${=}32$, 3 epochs, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
After gold-filtering (removing instances with no gold entities), the evaluation set contains $n{=}32{,}565$ instances across 8 coarse entity types; 11.9\% receive zero F1 under greedy decoding.

\paragraph{Key observations.}
(1)~All five signals achieve positive QE ($\rho$ 0.29--0.42); quality estimation works on Few-NERD. LP leads ($\rho{=}0.42$), followed by VC ($0.39$); the ranking differs from SciERC where VC leads, consistent with dataset-specific signal informativeness.
(2)~LP is the only signal achieving significant positive selection ($+1.39$~pp, $p{<}0.001$, CI excludes zero). The sample-level AUROC of 0.578 confirms LP provides per-sample discriminability beyond instance-level quality prediction.
(3)~Despite positive $\rho$, all structural signals degrade selection ($-1.79$ to $-3.85$~pp), further confirming that the correlation-selection gap is not an artifact of weak QE.
(4)~Low degeneracy (13.8\%) combined with strong LP-quality alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$) enables LP selection: candidates differ in F1 more often, and LP can rank them effectively. This contrasts with SciERC (17.8\% degeneracy but weak alignment $\rho{\approx}0.24$, LP $+0.61$~pp) and CoNLL (48.4\%, LP $-0.85$~pp).

The degeneracy-gating mechanism holds at entity-type granularity: 7 of 8 types show positive LP selection gains, and the sole negative type (Art, $-0.17$~pp) has the highest degeneracy (19.8\%).
The correlation between per-type degeneracy and oracle headroom is strong and significant (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$; exact permutation $p{=}0.005$); degeneracy directly constrains the headroom available for selection.
Under a conservative $\text{df}{=}4$ adjustment for within-type dependence, the correlation remains significant ($p{=}0.033$).
Entity types show near-zero intra-class correlation (ICC $= -0.004$), supporting the independence assumption underlying per-type analysis.
